newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian leader says foreigners in "terror" plot.
newsitem.headline: Algerian leader says foreigners in "terror" plot.

text.p: Algerian President Liamine Zeroual on Friday accused unnamed foreigners of being behind "terror and fear" in Algeria where over 200 people have been killed in two weeks of attacks blamed on Moslem fundamentalists.
He vowed to crush what he termed a conspiracy manipulated from outside and reiterated that attacks on isolated villages and bombings showed that the "terrorists" had failed.

In a 20-minute nationwide broadcast on television, Zeroual vowed: "I confirm to the dear Algerian people the determination of the Algerian state to battle against the terrorist groups until their final eradication."
Zeroual said Algeria would pursue its course to elections, pluralism and democracy but gave no date for a general election he has promised will be held in the first half of this year.
The president's address followed bombs in and near Algiers, and massacres in villages blamed by the authorities on Moslem rebels.

Zeroual said the people had a right to know about the events and the state's plans for their security. He gave no details of the recent killings, the latest of which, residents say, came on Thursday night when 15 civilians were slaughtered and mutilated. Ten of those were women.
The president said he "offered his sincere condolences to the families and relatives of the victims and assured them of the solidarity of all the Algerian people".
Zeroual, in dark suit and flanked by the green and white Algerian flag, said foreigners wanted to destabilise Algeria.

In an apparent swipe at Algeria's legal opposition leaders, such as war veteran Hocine Ait Ahmed, head of the Socialist Forces Front (FFS), the president warned that for "all those who try in vain, inside and outside Algeria, to hinder its march, Algeria is determined to complete its electoral process and national recovery".
Ait Ahmed on Thursday urged U.S. President Bill Clinton to appoint a mediator to help end the spiral of violence.

The Algerian authorities have consistently rejected what they term "outside interference" in their crisis. This erupted early in 1992 after they cancelled a general election in which Islamists had taken a commanding lead. About 60,000 people have since died.
Zeroual emphasised repeatedly that Algeria would defeat what he called "terrorism and barbarian violence".

He condemned those who "hide today under the cover of calls for peace -- calls whose sole truth lies in an invitation to the Algerian people to resign themselves to assassinations, destruction and hegemony".
Without naming any country or side, but in an apparent reference to a meeting in Rome at the end of 1994, he said:
"These crimes have coincided with a conspiracy in which foreign circles and Algerian personalities took part during a meeting held abroad."

The Rome meeting was attended by the FFS and the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), which had dominated the December 1991 general election. The meeting concluded with a conditional offer to Algiers to negotiate a way out of the crisis.
Zeroual blamed "bands of criminals, traitors and mercenaries manipulated by external circles who are exploiting their savagery to serve foreign interests".

Since January 10, when the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan started, more than 200 people have been killed in bomb attacks on the capital and in massacres near Algiers. The Armed Islamic Group (GIA) had vowed to increase their attacks during Ramadan.

Residents said on Friday the latest massacre was of 15 civilians on a farm just outside the capital on Thursday night. An unconfirmed report circulating in Algiers said another 22 died on an attack on an isolated community on Wednesday night.
The GIA is the most radical of the fundamentalists who took up arms after the Algerian authorities scrapped the general election.
